newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croat police blamed for shooting incident.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croat police blamed for shooting incident.

text.p: International police investigators reported on Tuesday that Bosnian Croat police fired on unarmed Moslems without cause and behaved in a criminal manner in an incident earlier this month in the divided town of Mostar.

"The use by law enforcement officers of excessive force in beating marchers, and of unnecessary and disproportionate lethal force, resulted in one death and numerous injuries," the international police report, obtained by Reuters, said.

The investigation, conducted by a team of monitors from the International Police Task Force (IPTF), said two Croat police were photographed firing into a crowd of retreating Moslems who had tried to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar.
One of the policeman was identified as Ivan Hrkac, deputy chief of police in western Mostar, the report said.
Witnesses said a third policeman in plainclothes was seen firing into the crowd. Three other policemen were photographed with their weapons drawn, according to the report.
The February 10 attack, which left one Moslem man dead and at least 20 wounded, marked the most serious violence to erupt in Bosnia since a peace agreement was signed in December 1995.

Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, met leaders of the Moslem-Croat federation and demanded Croat authorities immediately press charges against the policemen who fired on the marchers.
"Those policemen identified as taking part in the shooting should be dismissed from office, should be arrested and should be prosecuted," Steiner told reporters.

But Steiner said the Croat member of the collective presidency, Kresimir Zubak, failed to agree to prompt action. He proposed a wider investigation which would examine events that preceded the February 10 incident.
Steiner said Zubak's response was "not acceptable" and that prosecuting crimes was not up for negotiation.
"Crime must be prosecuted...We have proof and the authorities have to act accordingly," he said.
The German diplomat said the High Represenative and other international agencies in Bosnia would convey the Croat response to the major powers' Contact Group.
"We will now inform the Contact Group ....what we got as a reaction from the Croat side. And we will seek the full political backing for these demands," Steiner said.

The investigation concluded that the Croat police had been informed beforehand about the planned procession and had assigned police to the route near the Liska cemetery, where Moslems and Croats are buried side by side.

After the incident, Croat police launched a "concerted effort" to cover-up the facts of the attack, with Croat police chief Marko Radic and other officers presenting false information to IPTF investigators, the report said.
Their behaviour "reflects the absence of professional leadership at the highest level in the west Mostar police", it said.
Croat authorities have suspended six policemen over the incident but have also pressed charges against Moslems, alleging they had provoked the violence.
Violence in Mostar has damaged already strained relations within the Moslem-Croat federation, which together with the Serb republic comprises peacetime Bosnia.
